html:
The journey of William of Rubruck, a Franciscan friar from Flanders, to the court of the Great Khan Möngke of the Mongol Empire in 1253 to 1255. His report to King Louis IX of France is the best early Western account of the Mongols.

He left Constantinople in 1253, crossed the steppe in great hardship, and reached Möngke's camp at the end of the year. He spent part of 1254 at Karakorum, the Mongol capital, where he found a mixed world: Chinese, Muslims, Buddhists, Nestorian Christians of the Church of the East, and even a Parisian goldsmith who had built a silver tree that poured drinks. Möngke held a debate between the faiths, which William joined.

He made no converts and won no alliance for the crusade. But his Latin report is sharp and exact: he correctly said the Caspian is a closed sea and described the Mongols' customs and religions. Roger Bacon used it. It was written two decades before Marco Polo set out.
